p.x:
I work in an office in Bangkok. I start work at 8:30. First, I check my emails and look at the notice board for news. Then I make a list of my tasks for the day.
In the morning, I usually print some files. Our printer is old and often runs out of paper, so I have to fill it many times! I also use a stapler a lot to put the pages together.
At 12:00, I have a one-hour lunch break. I usually eat with my colleagues in a small restaurant near the office. In the afternoon, I answer phone calls and help customers. Some of my friends work shifts, but I always finish at 5:30. I like my job because my colleagues are friendly.

Last summer, I worked as an intern in the marketing department of a big company. On my first day, I was nervous. The office was open-plan, with no walls between desks, and there were about fifty people. Every morning, we had to clock in with a card at the entrance.
My manager, Ms Jane, was in charge of a new project for an important client. She gave me small jobs at first: making copies on the photocopier, ordering stationery and writing the minutes during meetings. Later, she asked me to put sales numbers into a spreadsheet and help with a presentation.
Every Monday, we had a meeting with a clear agenda. Sometimes we would brainstorm ideas for adverts. I learned that working in an office means you must multitask: answering emails, preparing documents and talking to colleagues at the same time.
At the end of my internship, I had an appraisal with Ms Jane. She gave me useful feedback and said I was a fast learner. The company even had flexitime, so I could start late if I had a class. One colleague was on sick leave for a week, so I helped her team too. Some older staff still worked in a cubicle, and one sent a memo every Friday!

The traditional office, with its fixed desks, rigid hierarchy and nine-to-five routine, is changing rapidly. Many companies have replaced private offices with open-plan spaces, and some have introduced hot-desking, in which employees choose a different desk each day. Supporters argue that these arrangements encourage collaboration and save money on space. Critics respond that they increase noise, reduce privacy and make it harder to concentrate.
Technology has transformed office life even more. Paper documents that once filled a filing cabinet are now stored in the cloud, and a videoconference can connect colleagues on different continents in seconds. Since the pandemic, many companies have adopted hybrid models, with staff working partly from home. Surveys suggest that many employees value this flexibility because it improves their work-life balance.
Yet something may have been lost. Informal conversations by the water cooler or in the staff room, which once helped spread ideas and build relationships, happen less often when people are not physically together. Some managers, worried about productivity, have responded by monitoring employees closely, a tendency to micromanage that often damages trust.
The human side of work remains important. Office politics, the competition for influence and recognition, exists online as much as in person, and HR departments increasingly focus on wellbeing and fairness. Meanwhile, employees everywhere still complain about red tape: the forms, approvals and procedures that slow decisions down. The office of the future, it seems, will need to combine flexibility with genuine human connection.
